timeline.draft_answer: The catastrophic double glacier collapse in Tibet in 2016 was investigated by an international team of researchers from ETH Zurich (the Earth Observation and Remote Sensing Group and the Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology - VAW), the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF, and the GAPHAZ commission (Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains). They analyzed numerous satellite images and used the SLF-developed simulation software RAMMS (Rapid Mass Movements) to reproduce the avalanche. After the first ice avalanche on 17 July 2016, they detected a fracture line on a neighboring glacier nearly identical to the one where the 'northern twin' had broken off, indicating a second collapse was imminent. Yves Bühler and colleagues modeled the risk and created a hazard map, and the warning was forwarded via GAPHAZ to Chinese scientists and local authorities in Tibet. A few hours later, on 22 September 2016, the second collapse occurred as predicted. The investigation suggests that geological and topographical factors, meteorological conditions, and most likely recent climate changes played a role in why two neighboring glaciers collapsed in such a similar way and close in time. The rapid satellite-based analysis was considered a milestone in the development of early warning systems.
